thread.title: Vote 'No' on Amendment 1

title: Vote 'No' on Amendment 1
text: Tennesseans will vote on three constitutional amendments in the upcoming November ballot. The first amendment proposes changing something the early settlers brought with them before Tennessee became a state. Amendment 1 seeks to limit the right to bail. The ballot will specify a short list of serious crimes, including acts of terrorism, second-degree murder, aggravated rape of a child, aggravated rape, and grave torture. Almost no one argues for an absolute right to bail in those cases. But the amendment's scope goes far beyond this list. It will also eliminate the right to bail for any crime that requires serving at least 85% of a prison sentence, a list the legislature built years ago for entirely different reasons. That list consists of 73 felonies. None of these will be named on the ballot. Some charges on that list are serious, but others may result in only probation. All of these charges can be brought against people who might later be found not guilty, have their cases dismissed, or plead to lesser charges. Yet, you will be asked to vote on this entire list without seeing it. The words Amendment 1 would rewrite have been in the Tennessee Constitution since 1796. Tennessee's settlers brought these words with them. Congress ensured these rights for the people living in what became Tennessee, and our framers adopted the language from Pennsylvania, which originally came from William Penn. Tennessee has had three constitutions, and each has kept this language. For 230 years, no legislature has dared to alter it. I acknowledge that some people may need to be held before trial. Between 2015 and 2018, I prosecuted white-collar crimes and elder abuse in Knox County. That means I handled cases involving victims who couldn't protect themselves. My perspective on who should be released from court is not sentimental. There are certainly cases where no conditions or security can ensure the safety of witnesses or families. That is not the question. The question is whether it is fair to take something away from all Tennesseans in order to detain a few more people. It is not. And besides, the Constitution is not the problem. Prosecutors and judges already have the tools to hold those who need to be held. Judges decide who gets released and under what conditions. Since 2024, judges must put community safety first and impose monitoring requirements on those released on conditions. The same law makes violating a release condition a separate crime. Speaker Sexton says the amendment preserves judicial discretion, and he is right. But that means the amendment adds just one new power: the ability to deny bail based solely on the charge, before the evidence has been tested. I don't know about you, but I'm not comfortable with incarceration based on an accusation alone. Or punishment without trial. Here is what the campaign for this amendment leaves out: If a judge makes a bad bail decision, prosecutors can appeal. Prosecutors have been able to do this for years. And the process is built for speed: no briefs, no oral arguments, and the appellate court must rule "promptly." The Tennessee Supreme Court has described this appeal as the "only effective remedy" for bad bail decisions. But prosecutors are not using this tool. Last year, appellate courts handled just 26 bail appeals across 95 counties, including those filed by the accused. In that same year, Tennessee's criminal courts recorded over 150,000 filings. That is not a broken constitution. Before tinkering with fundamental liberty, maybe the government should try using the tools at its disposal. Supporters argue that people released on bond commit new crimes, and some do, but they are the exception. According to the most recent comprehensive national study of felony cases in large counties, only 16% of people released before trial were arrested for any offense before their cases concluded, and only 8% were arrested for a new felony. Sure, 8% is not zero, but it is also not enough reason to amend our Bill of Rights. The data shows another important finding: those held in jail until their cases concluded were convicted 77% of the time, while those released pre-trial were convicted only 59% of the time, despite facing the same charges. A person incarcerated while awaiting trial risks losing their job, housing, and motivation to continue fighting their case. When prosecutors offer time served, many will take the deal, irrespective of their guilt. Around 20% of the people on the national registry of exonerations originally pled guilty. Detention does not predict a conviction. It manufactures one. The founders of this state did not write the bail clause because they trusted every accused person. They wrote it because they distrusted every government, including one made of people they liked. The rule they inherited was that it "is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer." Our legislature is asking you to flip that principle on its head but leaving much of what the amendment would actually do off the ballot. I understand the impulse. I read the same news you do. But a constitution is not a mood. It is the thing that holds when the mood passes. Vote 'No' on Amendment 1. Willie Santana is a former Tennessee prosecutor and currently serves as an assistant federal defender.

But that means the amendment adds just one new power: the ability to deny bail based solely on the charge, before the evidence has been tested.
